documents.unit: Dean of Students, Office of Student Rights and Responsibilities
documents.title: AI Academic Misconduct
documents.summary: Faculty-facing guidance from the student conduct office on academic misconduct. It lists unauthorized AI use as misconduct but sets no university stance on AI, telling faculty to state in their syllabus whether AI is allowed. The rest covers communicating expectations, assessment design, reporting and the conduct process.
documents.stance_why: The page never says AI is allowed or banned. It lists 'Unauthorized use of artificial intelligence' as misconduct and says faculty 'should clearly state: Whether AI tools are permitted' and 'course-specific expectations (i.e. acceptable A.I. Use)', so the decision is delegated to instructors.

units.why: Opening rationale: academic integrity 'grounded in honesty, trust, fairness, respect and responsibility' is the reason given for the page's rules, so it is a fairness/honesty rationale (P95), not skill-building (P41).
units.anchor: supports a learning environment grounded in honesty, trust, fairness, respect and responsibility

units.why: Faculty are 'expected to' communicate academic expectations; this binds instructors to make rules explicit, closest to P09, but it covers academic expectations generally, not AI or a syllabus specifically.
units.anchor: Clearly communicate academic expectations
units.policy: Faculty are expected to clearly communicate academic expectations.
units.fit_note: Does not mention AI or the syllabus; general academic expectations.

units.why: 'Submit reports when violations are suspected' is a duty on faculty to file reports, the procedural step after suspected misconduct (P81).
units.anchor: Submit reports when violations are suspected
units.policy: Faculty are expected to submit reports when violations are suspected.

units.why: The list of academic misconduct includes 'Unauthorized use of artificial intelligence or online resources', classifying unauthorized AI use as misconduct (P36).
units.anchor: Unauthorized use of artificial intelligence or online resources
units.policy: Academic misconduct may include unauthorized use of artificial intelligence or online resources.

units.why: Faculty 'are encouraged to' clarify 'expectations regarding AI tools, online resources, and citation practices' at the start; this is communicating AI expectations (P09), partly fitted since it is encouraged and not tied to the syllabus.
units.anchor: Clarify expectations regarding AI tools, online resources, and citation practices
units.policy: Faculty are encouraged to clarify expectations regarding AI tools, online resources, and citation practices.
units.fit_note: Encouraged rather than required, and not specifically tied to the syllabus.

units.why: Faculty are encouraged to 'Discuss expectations before major assignments or exams', going beyond a syllabus line to repeated discussion with students (P66).
units.anchor: Discuss expectations before major assignments or exams
units.policy: Faculty are encouraged to discuss academic integrity expectations before major assignments or exams.
units.fit_note: About integrity expectations in general, not only AI.

units.why: 'Clearly communicating expectations can help prevent misunderstandings and reduce unintentional violations' states why expectations should be communicated; it is a prevention rationale, nearest P99 (reducing causes of misuse).
units.anchor: Clearly communicating expectations can help prevent misunderstandings and reduce unintentional violations.
units.fit_note: Prevention by clear communication rather than by easing pressures.

units.why: Faculty 'are encouraged to include a syllabus statement' that 'Explains course-specific expectations (i.e. acceptable A.I. Use)'; this asks for a syllabus statement covering AI (P09).
units.anchor: Explains course-specific expectations (i.e. acceptable A.I. Use)
units.policy: Faculty are encouraged to include in the syllabus a statement that explains course-specific expectations, i.e. acceptable A.I. use.

units.why: The syllabus statement is to outline 'possible academic consequences', a communication of sanctions in advance; it names no specific penalty, so P37 fits only partly.
units.anchor: Outlines possible academic consequences
units.policy: The syllabus statement outlines possible academic consequences.
units.fit_note: Says consequences should be outlined but states none.

units.why: The syllabus 'areas to clarify' include 'Use of generative AI tools', leaving the decision of what is allowed to each course, so P04.
units.anchor: Use of generative AI tools
units.policy: Use of generative AI tools is an area faculty should clarify in the course syllabus.

units.why: The university does not set a stance: 'faculty should clearly state: Whether AI tools are permitted', so the permit/prohibit decision sits with the instructor (P04).
units.anchor: faculty should clearly state:
units.policy: Faculty should clearly state whether AI tools are permitted.

units.why: Faculty should state 'What types of assistance are allowed', so the allowed uses of AI are set per course (P04).
units.anchor: What types of assistance are allowed
units.policy: Faculty should clearly state what types of assistance are allowed.

units.why: Faculty should state 'Citation expectations for AI-generated content'; this leaves the citation rule to the instructor, so it is partly P24 (disclosure) but sets no citation requirement itself.
units.anchor: Citation expectations for AI-generated content
units.policy: Faculty should clearly state citation expectations for AI-generated content.
units.fit_note: Instructors decide whether and how to cite; the university requires no disclosure.

units.why: 'Students should not be expected to guess what is or is not permitted in a course' is the principle behind requiring clear statements, closest to P09.
units.anchor: should not be expected to guess what is or is not permitted in a course
units.fit_note: Principle that supports stating rules; does not itself require a syllabus statement.

units.why: 'Because technology and AI tools continue to evolve' ties the advice to change over time; this is a short acknowledgement of change (P54) but not a commitment to revise.
units.anchor: Because technology and AI tools continue to evolve
units.policy: Technology and AI tools continue to evolve.
units.fit_note: Acknowledges change in tools; no review cycle for the policy.

units.why: 'Using varied or personalized assignment prompts' is an assessment-design response to reduce misconduct, so P35.
units.anchor: Using varied or personalized assignment prompts
units.policy: Faculty can reduce opportunities for misconduct by using varied or personalized assignment prompts.

units.why: 'Structuring assessments that emphasize process over memorization' redesigns assessment around process, matching P35.
units.anchor: Structuring assessments that emphasize process over memorization
units.policy: Faculty can reduce opportunities for misconduct by structuring assessments that emphasize process over memorization.

units.why: 'Utilizing question banks and randomized testing' is an exam-security design suggestion; it is not about AI specifically and fits no type, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: Utilizing question banks and randomized testing
units.policy: Faculty can reduce opportunities for misconduct by utilizing question banks and randomized testing.
units.uncovered_note: Exam-design tactics (question banks, randomized tests) to reduce misconduct.

units.why: 'Academic pressure, time management difficulties, and stress can contribute to misconduct' and faculty should remind students of resources: prevention by easing pressures (P99).
units.anchor: Faculty are encouraged to remind students about available resources
units.policy: Faculty are encouraged to remind students about available resources such as tutoring, writing assistance, office hours and counseling, because academic pressure, time management difficulties and stress can contribute to misconduct.

units.why: Lists 'Tutoring and academic support services', 'Writing assistance', 'Office hours' as support to direct students to: human help (P72).
units.anchor: Tutoring and academic support services
units.policy: Faculty remind students of available resources including tutoring and academic support services, writing assistance and office hours.

units.why: 'Faculty are encouraged to communicate with the student before submitting a report' is the talk-first practice (P57).
units.anchor: faculty are encouraged to communicate with the student before submitting a report

units.why: The conversation should 'Allow the student an opportunity to respond', a right-to-respond element (P64).
units.anchor: Allow the student an opportunity to respond
units.policy: The conversation with the student before a report allows the student an opportunity to respond.

units.why: 'Faculty should remain professional, objective and focused on the observed behavior' sets an evidence-based stance toward suspected misuse; P69 fits only partly since it names no standard of proof.
units.anchor: remain professional, objective and focused on the observed behavior and available information
units.fit_note: Asks for objectivity but states no evidence standard.

units.why: Reports should include 'Student name(s)... Supporting documentation', specifying what a report contains, the formal reporting procedure (P81).
units.anchor: When reporting suspected academic misconduct, include:
units.policy: When reporting suspected academic misconduct, faculty include student names, course and assignment information, a description, relevant dates and supporting documentation.

units.why: Supporting documentation examples include 'Turnitin or plagiarism reports' and 'Canvas activity logs': similarity checks and process evidence used to identify misuse (P40).
units.anchor: Turnitin or plagiarism reports
units.policy: Examples of supporting documentation for a misconduct report include Turnitin or plagiarism reports, screenshots, exam comparisons and Canvas activity logs.

units.why: 'Reports should be submitted as promptly as possible after discovery' is a deadline in the reporting procedure (P81).
units.anchor: Reports should be submitted as promptly as possible after discovery of the concern.
units.policy: Faculty submit reports of suspected academic misconduct through the appropriate university reporting process, as promptly as possible after discovery.

units.why: After a report 'The student is notified of the allegation' and informed of rights; describes the office's procedure, P81 as the nearest type.
units.anchor: The student is notified of the allegation
units.policy: Once a report is received, the Office of Student Rights and Responsibilities reviews it and notifies the student of the allegation, the process and their rights.
units.fit_note: Describes what the office does after a report rather than what faculty must do.

units.why: Students are 'typically provided an opportunity to... Respond to the information presented', the right to respond (P64).
units.anchor: Respond to the information presented
units.policy: Students are typically provided an opportunity to review the allegation, respond to the information presented, share their perspective and participate in the resolution process.

units.why: 'The conduct process is educational in nature' frames the response to misconduct as educational (P68).
units.anchor: The conduct process is educational in nature
units.policy: The conduct process is educational in nature and seeks to balance accountability, fairness, and student development.

units.why: 'Faculty generally retain authority over academic decisions', listing grade reductions, assignment or course failure as outcomes: possible penalties are named though not tied to offense level (P37).
units.anchor: Faculty generally retain authority over academic decisions within the course
units.policy: Faculty generally retain authority over academic decisions within the course, including grade reductions, assignment failure, course failure and alternative academic remedies consistent with university policy.
units.fit_note: Lists the range of possible outcomes, no specific penalty for AI misuse.

units.why: Outcomes must consider 'mitigating and aggravating circumstances such as prior conduct history or egregiousness'; no type covers weighing circumstances in sanctions.
units.anchor: consider mitigating and aggravating circumstances such as prior conduct history
units.policy: Faculty consider mitigating and aggravating circumstances, such as prior conduct history or egregiousness of the alleged violation, in determining outcomes.
units.uncovered_note: Weigh mitigating and aggravating circumstances when deciding sanctions.

units.why: 'Avoid making assumptions before reviewing all available information' guards against premature conclusions in suspected cases; close to P69 but sets no evidence standard.
units.anchor: Avoid making assumptions before reviewing all available information
units.policy: Faculty and staff are encouraged to avoid making assumptions before reviewing all available information.
units.fit_note: Procedural caution, not a standard of proof.

units.why: 'Maintain confidentiality throughout the process' is a conduct-process rule that fits no existing type.
units.anchor: Maintain confidentiality throughout the process
units.policy: Faculty and staff are encouraged to maintain confidentiality throughout the misconduct process.
units.uncovered_note: Keep confidentiality during academic misconduct cases.

units.why: 'Consult with the Office of Student Rights and Responsibilities when questions arise' names the office that advises on cases; nearest P80 (who owns/enforces).
units.anchor: Consult with the Office of Student Rights and Responsibilities when questions arise
units.fit_note: Names a consultation office, not an owner of the AI policy.

units.why: The office offers 'Academic integrity presentations for students or departments', training on integrity for students and staff (P70).
units.anchor: Academic integrity presentations for students or departments
units.policy: The Office of Student Rights and Responsibilities provides academic integrity presentations for students or departments.

units.why: The office offers 'Support with syllabus language and prevention strategies' and consultation, which helps faculty set course policy (P63).
units.anchor: Support with syllabus language and prevention strategies
units.policy: The Office of Student Rights and Responsibilities provides support with syllabus language and prevention strategies.
units.fit_note: Support is about integrity and syllabus language generally, not learning AI.

units.why: 'Dishonesty can negatively impact peers and classroom trust' grounds the rules in fairness and community trust (P95).
units.anchor: Dishonesty can negatively impact peers and classroom trust
units.policy: Faculty may wish to emphasize that dishonesty can negatively impact peers and classroom trust.

units.why: Faculty 'may wish to emphasize' why integrity matters to students, i.e. explain the reasons behind rules (P66).
units.anchor: Students are more likely to make ethical decisions when they understand the broader impact
units.policy: Faculty may explain why academic integrity matters because students are more likely to make ethical decisions when they understand the broader impact of academic misconduct.
units.fit_note: About academic integrity generally, not AI rules.

notes: Single university-level page; navigation text skipped. Some units are general integrity guidance coded because they sit on the AI misconduct page; several are fit_note cases because they are not AI-specific.
